papers.title: IsaGraphLib: Formally Verified Efficient Graph Algorithms in Isabelle/HOL
papers.abstract: We present a library of formally verified graph algorithms in Isabelle/HOL. The library covers the main problems of combinatorial optimisation on graphs: reachability, shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, matching, maximum flow, and minimum-cost flow. The algorithms in the library use most of the standard algorithm design techniques: graph search, greedy algorithms on matroids, dynamic programming, augmenting paths, blossom contraction, blocking flows, push-relabel, scaling, the primal-dual method, randomisation, and certificate checking. The library has adaptors between different types of graphs (directed, undirected, multigraphs), which allow results to be reused. Each algorithm is verified independently of its data structures, and the main algorithms are refined to efficient imperative implementations, from which we generate code in Standard ML, Scala, and Go. We developed parts of the library with large language models (LLMs), improved the quality of their proofs with a method based on statistics of our own proofs, and labelled which parts were developed by humans, by LLMs, or collaboratively. We perform a detailed experimental analysis of representative algorithms in our library, comparing it with state-of-the-art mainstream libraries, showing that our implementations are practical.

papers.title: Providing Accuracy Guarantees for the Fixed-Point Emulation of Matrix Multiplication
papers.abstract: Fixed-point methods such as Ozaki-II emulate double-precision matrix multiplication (GEMM) on fast low-precision hardware. Software that chooses the mantissa bit count automatically is numerically safe when the emulated product keeps the error guarantee of the floating-point GEMM it replaces. We analyze the worst-case and average-case error of fixed-point and floating-point dot products, define exponent span capacities that determine the extra mantissa bits an input requires, and approximate them with a low-precision GEMM. We prove that 53 bits plus such a capacity and a small constant preserve the classical worst-case error bound for a floating-point dot product, and we demonstrate this guarantee in software on several test cases. In a developer build of cuBLAS on an NVIDIA B200, each implemented bit-count rule earns grade~A on Test~2c of ``Grading the BLAS'' at every size and exponent range tested, falling back to double precision at the widest ranges; in exact arithmetic, the bound holds on every adversarial and random input tested.

papers.title: Discontinuity-Aware Solvers for Vapor-Compression Cycles
papers.abstract: Physics-based models of vapor-compression cycles are often formulated as large, stiff DAE systems with derivative discontinuities introduced at the points of phase change. We use an implementation of a discontinuity-aware ODE and DAE solver scheme that uses domain-specific, user-declared information to compute appropriate time steps for more efficient integration. This scheme is made open-source within DifferentialEquations.jl. We demonstrate how discontinuity information can be specified symbolically in a declarative modeling language such as Dyad and passed to the solver to address the numerical challenges posed. We apply this discontinuity-aware technique to two applications: first, a scalar ODE with two discontinuities, and then a model of a full vapor-compression cycle. The discontinuity-aware solver yields significantly fewer step rejections and improved solver times, particularly with the Rodas5P solver at loose tolerances, as compared to standard error control, suggesting that exposing physical discontinuity information from equation-oriented models to adaptive solvers can improve practical simulation performance without requiring reassembly of the model.

papers.title: Trustworthy Numerical Software in the Age of AI: What Would Turing Do?
papers.abstract: AI coding agents can now produce numerical software faster than human experts can review it, raising serious concerns about usability and reliability. These and other AI tools are already transforming mathematics and software, and they will soon transform mathematical software. These concerns motivated us to assess AI-generated numerical linear algebra (NLA) kernels, which we did through an audit of a recent public GPU QR competition. All five leading kernels passed the competition's accuracy tests, and the winning kernel achieved a 107-fold speedup over the competition's baseline, which calls NVIDIA's QR routine. Yet each failed at least once on new inputs, even those from the competition's generator, under the same checker, while the baseline passed them all. In light of this, we want to develop reusable formalizations of numerical analysis methods, which remain sparsely represented in existing formal libraries. We describe VSCL, our Lean library of mathematical foundations for numerical computing. We also propose VERNA to connect these tasks by using formalized results to guide kernel assessment against explicit specifications. Drawing on Turing's work on rounding-error analysis and program checking, we discuss design principles for developing trustworthy numerical software when direct human checking is impractical.
